name: ML Pipeline Infrastructure (MLOps)
description: Design an end-to-end ML pipeline infrastructure. Covers data ingestion, feature engineering, model training, model registry, serving infrastructure, and monitoring.

learnSteps.title: Data Ingestion and Feature Engineering
learnSteps.description: The Data Ingestion pipeline (Spark) runs daily, pulling raw data from upstream sources, cleaning and transforming it, and writing curated datasets to the Data Lake (S3) as Parquet files partitioned by date. It also computes and materializes features into the Feature Store (Redis) for low-latency online serving. Feature engineering logic is versioned and tested alongside model code to ensure reproducibility.

learnSteps.title: Model Training and Experimentation
learnSteps.description: The Training Cluster reads curated datasets from S3 and trains models on GPU instances. Hyperparameter tuning runs multiple experiments in parallel. Training metrics (loss, accuracy, AUC) are tracked by Prometheus and logged to an experiment tracker. Once a model meets quality thresholds, it is serialized (ONNX/TorchScript) and pushed to the Model Registry with metadata (training data version, hyperparameters, metrics).

learnSteps.title: Model Serving and Inference
learnSteps.description: The Model Serving API loads the latest approved model from the Registry on startup. It receives prediction requests, fetches real-time features from the Feature Store, and delegates to the Inference Engine (GPU) for computation. Batch requests are dynamically grouped for GPU efficiency. Blue-green deployment ensures zero-downtime model updates. The Serving API supports A/B testing by routing traffic percentages to different model versions.

learnSteps.title: Monitoring and Model Drift Detection
learnSteps.description: Prometheus collects serving metrics (latency, throughput, error rate) and model quality metrics (prediction distribution, feature drift scores). Data drift is detected by comparing live feature distributions against training data statistics. When drift exceeds thresholds, alerts trigger and the pipeline can automatically kick off retraining. This closed loop ensures models stay accurate as real-world data evolves over time.

chaosScenarios.name: Inference GPU Queue Saturation
chaosScenarios.description: A traffic spike saturates the GPU inference fleet; dynamic batching queues grow faster than autoscaling can add nodes
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Batch queue depth climbs; p99 inference latency degrades from ~180ms to seconds, then serving-app requests time out. GPU autoscaling lags 5-10 minutes behind demand because node provisioning and model loading are slow.
mitigationSteps: Enable request shedding with a hard queue-depth cap (fast-fail beats slow-fail)
Fail over to the distilled fallback model on CPU for shed traffic
Scale from the pre-provisioned warm GPU pool
Review batching parameters — larger batches raise throughput at p99 cost

chaosScenarios.name: Feature Store Outage
chaosScenarios.description: The Redis feature store crashes; online feature lookups fail at request time
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Depending on policy, predictions either fail outright or silently degrade using default/stale feature values. The silent path is the dangerous one: latency and error dashboards stay green while prediction quality tanks.
mitigationSteps: Fail over to the feature store replica
If degraded mode is enabled, tag every prediction served with default features
Watch prediction distribution metrics for shift — not just error rates
Backfill features and verify freshness before clearing the incident

chaosScenarios.name: Regressed Model Version Promoted
chaosScenarios.description: A corrupted or quality-regressed model version is promoted from the registry to serving
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: The nastiest ML failure mode: latency normal, error rate zero, predictions confidently wrong. Only model-quality metrics in Prometheus (drift score, prediction distribution, downstream conversion) reveal the regression.
mitigationSteps: Freeze the rollout and pin traffic to the previous registry version
Trigger automatic rollback via the canary quality gate
Verify artifact checksum against the registry record
Replay canary traffic offline to characterize the regression before re-promoting

bottleneckProgression.description: GPU dynamic-batching queue saturates; inference latency degrades superlinearly past the knee
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add GPU replicas, tune batch size/timeout, distill or quantize the model

bottleneckProgression.description: Per-request feature vector fan-out (hundreds of features per prediction) saturates Redis network throughput
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Shard the cluster, compress feature vectors, cache slow-moving features client-side

bottleneckProgression.description: Pre/post-processing and gRPC serialization saturate the serving API tier
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale horizontally; move heavy transforms offline into the feature pipeline

expectedIssues.title: Training/Serving Skew
expectedIssues.description: Features computed in Spark offline differ subtly from the online serving path, silently degrading accuracy
expectedIssues.mitigation: Single shared transform library for both paths; continuous skew monitoring comparing online vs offline feature distributions

expectedIssues.title: Silent Data Drift
expectedIssues.description: Input distributions shift over weeks; the model degrades without throwing a single error
expectedIssues.mitigation: Drift detection on inputs and prediction distributions, scheduled retraining, champion/challenger evaluation

expectedIssues.title: Stale Online Features
expectedIssues.description: A delayed Spark pipeline run leaves the feature store serving features hours past their freshness SLA
expectedIssues.mitigation: Per-feature freshness SLAs with staleness metrics; streaming computation for time-sensitive features

expectedIssues.title: GPU Fleet Cost Creep
expectedIssues.description: Serving GPUs sized for peak sit idle off-peak; training jobs hold GPUs beyond need — spend dominates the platform budget
expectedIssues.mitigation: Queue-depth-based autoscaling with a small warm pool, spot instances for training, fractional GPUs (MIG) for small models

expectedIssues.title: Registry Metadata Desync
expectedIssues.description: Model artifact in S3 and registry metadata disagree (partial upload, stale pointer), so serving loads the wrong version
expectedIssues.mitigation: Immutable versioned artifacts, checksum validation at load time, registry as the single deployment source of truth

steps: Check GPU batch queue depth and utilization — saturation vs upstream slowness
Verify feature store lookup latency is normal (rule out the dependency)
Scale inference replicas from the warm pool
If the queue is not draining, enable the distilled fallback model for overflow traffic
Freeze the rollout and pin serving to the previous registry version
Confirm automatic rollback completed within the 5-minute SLA
Snapshot live inputs and predictions for offline analysis
Replay canary traffic against both versions to characterize the regression
Open a model incident review before re-promoting
Fail over to the Redis replica
Enable default-feature degraded mode with per-prediction tagging
Monitor prediction distribution for shift while degraded
Backfill features after recovery and verify freshness metrics
Check the Spark pipeline run status and failed partitions
Re-run failed partitions and validate freshness metrics recover
Notify model owners of the affected prediction window

decisions.title: Separate Training and Serving Infrastructure
decisions.context: Training is throughput-oriented batch work tolerant of interruption; serving is latency-critical and always-on — opposite scaling profiles
decisions.decision: Independent GPU pools: spot-friendly training cluster, latency-tuned serving fleet, with the model registry as the only contract between them
consequences: Training can use cheap interruptible capacity without risking serving SLOs
Each pool scales and is capacity-planned on its own signal
Model promotion becomes an explicit, auditable handoff through the registry

decisions.title: Online Feature Store Fed by the Offline Pipeline
decisions.context: The classic MLOps failure is computing features one way for training and another way for serving
decisions.decision: The same Spark pipeline that writes training data to the lake materializes online features into Redis
consequences: One computation path sharply reduces training/serving skew
Sub-millisecond feature lookups at inference time
Feature freshness is bounded by pipeline cadence and must be monitored as an SLA

decisions.title: Model Registry as the Deployment Gate
decisions.context: Models reaching production via ad-hoc copies are impossible to audit or roll back
decisions.decision: Serving loads only immutable, versioned, checksummed artifacts from the registry; promotion goes through canary quality gates
consequences: Instant rollback by repointing to the previous version
Full lineage from training run to serving deployment
Registry availability matters at deploy time only — not on the request path

decisions.title: Split Serving API From GPU Inference Engine
decisions.context: Pre/post-processing is CPU-bound and cheap to scale; GPU inference is expensive and batch-sensitive
decisions.decision: A CPU serving tier handles validation and feature assembly, calling the GPU engine over gRPC
consequences: GPU fleet sizes purely on inference load, maximizing utilization of the costliest resource
Dynamic batching can be tuned at the engine without touching API code
The extra hop adds ~1-2ms — negligible against the latency budget

tradeoffs.choice: Dynamic batching on the GPU engine
tradeoffs.benefit: 2-5x GPU throughput from amortizing kernel launches across batched requests
tradeoffs.cost: Batch-wait time directly inflates p99; batch size is a permanent tuning knob

tradeoffs.choice: Batch feature computation with streaming reserved for time-sensitive features
tradeoffs.benefit: Daily Spark batch is dramatically cheaper than streaming everything
tradeoffs.cost: Most features are hours stale; models must be trained to tolerate that staleness

alternatives.name: CPU Inference Inside the API Server
alternatives.description: Load the model into the API process and run inference on CPU — no GPU fleet, no gRPC hop
alternatives.prosVsCons: Radically simpler operations and lower fixed cost, but 10x+ latency for deep models and no independent scaling of inference
alternatives.whyNotChosen: The p99 latency target is unreachable on CPU for the model class being served

alternatives.name: Fully Managed Inference Endpoints
alternatives.description: Outsource serving to a managed platform (SageMaker-style endpoints)
alternatives.prosVsCons: Minimal ops burden and built-in autoscaling, but a significant cost premium and limited control over batching, multi-model packing, and warm pools
alternatives.whyNotChosen: At sustained 5k RPS the cost premium exceeds the ops savings, and batching control is needed to hit the latency target
